No dedicated bulk annual-return or PSC software was found.
- **CAC portal:** Free self-filing; agent or bulk features were not verified.
- **CAC reminders:** The CAC says it is building e-reminders for filing deadlines, working with NIBSS.
- **Manual agents:** Accredited agents and company-secretarial firms file for clients; Corporate Bestie, for example, advertises filing within 48 hours.
- **Content only:** Bumpa guides and a Paperform data-collection template.
- **Not found:** Searches for Lawpadi, Approve, Lawyard and Registrar-type platforms returned nothing.

result.duty:
Confirmed.
- **Annual returns:** CAMA 2020 s.417 requires every company, business name and incorporated trustee to file. Companies file within 42 days of the AGM or incorporation anniversary. Business names file by 30 June; Nairametrics, SCP Law and Bumpa all say so, so this no longer rests on one source.
- **Penalty:** s.425 makes the company and each director or officer liable. The CAC said it would apply the Companies Regulations 2021 penalties in full from 1 Jan 2024, later moved to 1 Apr 2024. One summary gives about N1,000 per day. For business names and incorporated trustees the penalty falls on the entity only.
- **Strike-off:** Failing to file for 10 consecutive years is a ground for strike-off.
- **Current round:** The CAC notice of 15 Jul 2026 (Nairametrics, 16 Jul) is the sixth batch under s.692(3),(4). It covers 100,000 companies, which must file outstanding returns and PSC information within 90 days, so by about 13 Oct 2026. Firms that miss it are struck off without further notice, and restoration needs a court order.
- **Not checked:** The letterhead rule under s.304(3) from 1 Aug 2026.
result.market:
- **Register size:** Daily Trust reported 3.1 million registered companies, a pre-2025 cumulative figure. No current official total was found.
- **Strike-offs:** The CAC struck off more than 400,000 companies in 2025, and 100,000 more are in the 2026 batch.
- **Active market:** Probably on the order of 1 to 2 million entities with a yearly filing duty (an unverified estimate). Many of them are dormant or informal and unlikely to pay.
result.reason: The duty is real and enforced. CAMA 2020 s.417 requires annual returns. s.425 makes the company and each director liable to prescribed penalties, applied in full since April 2024. The CAC's 15 Jul 2026 notice under s.692(3),(4) gives 100,000 firms 90 days to file outstanding returns and PSC information. Searches found no dedicated SaaS, only guides, the CAC's own self-file portal and manual accredited agents. But the strike-off window closes around 13 Oct 2026, four days from today, so that trigger has almost passed. Most firms on the list are dormant. Filing fees are small (₦3,000 to ₦5,000 for small entities), so customers will pay little. The CAC also plans its own e-reminders. A cheap agent-backed service could work; standalone software is a weak opportunity.

result.duty: Confirmed and in force: NTAA 2025 ss.13 and 14(3) require each individual with taxable income, including the self-employed, business owners and informal-sector traders, to file a return of total income with their state IRS within 90 days of the start of the assessment year. LIRS set 31 March 2026 for the 2025 income year, then extended it once to 14 April 2026. Penalties: s.101 fines non-filing or an inaccurate return N100,000 for the first month plus N50,000 for each further month. s.102 fines missing records N10,000 for individuals. Interest is charged at the CBN rate. Filing in Lagos is electronic only, through etax.lirs.net. The return is annual. Not checked: the s.147 small-business definition and how other states enforce the rules.

BusinessDay says informal and SME individuals make up most of about 4 million non-compliant taxpayers, but that figure is national and undated. Most of the potential market sits outside the tax net, and enforcement outside PAYE is weak.

result.reason: The duty is real and enforced. The Lagos State Safety Commission, acting under the Safety Commission Law No. 6 of 2011, required all lifts to be registered and certified by 31 March 2026. Around 30 April it sealed more than 12 malls, hotels and residential buildings and said enforcement would continue. No Nigeria-specific lift-compliance software turned up. Still, the free state portal handles registration, and global lift field-service and inspection apps (Klipboard, Caction, Lumiform) cover maintenance logs and reminders. The renewal interval, fees and contractor accreditation are unpublished, so the recurring part is unclear. The market is small: Lagos lift owners plus a few dozen lift contractors, with no count found. Buyers are concentrated and the main act is a one-off free registration, so the score is modest.

result.competitor: The free NELEX portal (nelex.gov.ng) handles online application, renewal and fee payment by card or Remita RRR. Licensing was digitised in April 2024. result.duty: Labour Act Cap L1 ss.23-25, 71 (federal, in force). Recruiter's Licence from the Federal Ministry of Labour and Employment. Fresh domestic licence N205,000 for 2 years. Renewal N105,000 for 1 year or N205,000 for 3 years. International licence N305,000 for 2 years. Renewal must be filed before expiry with NSITF registration and renewal evidence, PFA registration, bank guarantee or bond (N1.5m-5m domestic), client contracts, handbook and health insurance, plus a state labour office inspection. Ongoing duties: quarterly reports, routine inspection, annual PEA workshop, vacancies posted on NELEX. Incomplete files are returned. No specific fine was found for operating unlicensed. The NSITF judgment (NICN Awka, 4 June 2026) confirms Employees' Compensation Act enforcement but gives no penalty amounts.
result.market: Not found. No published count of licensed private employment agencies; the ministry and NELEX link a registered-PEA list but give no total. EAPEAN (formerly HuCaPAN) is the umbrella body of licensed PEAs, but its membership figure was not found. Rough estimate is hundreds to low thousands; unverified.
result.reason: The duty is real and federal. Sections 23-25 and 71 of the Labour Act require a Recruiter's Licence. Applications and renewals now go online through the ministry's NELEX portal: N5,000 application fee, then N100k-N300k per licence. Renewal is every 1, 2 or 3 years, plus quarterly reports and inspections. Renewal needs NSITF, PFA and client-contract evidence plus a bond; incomplete files are sent back. No licence or compliance tracker exists. Payroll tools (SeamlessHR, SoftSUITE) handle NSITF/ITF remittances, and NELEX handles submission. That leaves only document assembly and reminders: a thin MVP for an event every 1-3 years. No published count of licensed agencies; likely hundreds to low thousands. The EAPEAN association is a possible sales channel. Low frequency and low pain make it a weak standalone product, better as an add-on to K01 or payroll.

result.competitor: LIRS Eco Fiscal System (EFS), a free and mandatory state tool. It connects to the operator's POS, calculates the 5% tax, issues receipts with unique invoice numbers, sends sales to the LIRS Online Tax System in real time and keeps audit records. LIRS supplies a POS where an operator has none, and officials install the software on site. Hotel and POS vendors would also have to integrate with EFS. No third-party compliance tracker for the hospitality sector was found.
result.duty: Confirmed in force: Hotel Occupancy and Restaurant Consumption (HORC) Law 2009, Lagos State. A 5% consumption tax on goods and services sold in hotels, restaurants and event centres. Operators collect it as agents, must register with LIRS and remit monthly by the 20th of the following month. Late payment costs a 10% penalty plus interest at 5% above the CBN Monetary Policy Rate. LIRS has closed non-payers (16 firms in one case, 23 in another). The 2017 Fiscalisation Regulation requires EFS software, with penalties under s.11(2) of the 2009 law. Not verified: how the 2025 tax reform (Nigeria Tax Act) treats the levy. The Court of Appeal's ruling on the overlap with federal VAT also leaves its legal footing contested. The hotel-licensing, Lagos Safety Commission and NIHOTOUR duties were not checked.
result.market: Not found. No register count of Lagos hotels, restaurants and event centres registered for consumption tax turned up in the searches.
result.reason: The duty is real. The Lagos Hotel Occupancy and Restaurant Consumption Law 2009 sets a 5% tax, collected by the business as agent. Operators must register with LIRS and remit monthly by the 20th, or pay a 10% penalty plus interest; LIRS has closed non-payers. But LIRS already does the core job with its own mandatory Eco Fiscal System (EFS), under the 2017 Fiscalisation Regulation. EFS connects to the operator's POS, applies the rate automatically, issues numbered receipts and sends sales to the LIRS Online Tax System in real time. LIRS supplies a POS to operators who lack one and installs the software on site. That leaves little for a third-party tracker to do beyond licence reminders. Not checked: how the 2025 federal tax reform affects the Lagos levy. Not found: a count of affected businesses.

result.competitor: I found no dedicated tool that tracks NMDPRA licence and Weights and Measures certificate expiry, or keeps calibration records, for Nigerian stations. Several things partly overlap. NMDPRA's free ROMS portal handles new permits, renewals, payment and permit checks; it was not confirmed whether it sends expiry alerts. Fuelmetrics' Epump is a Nigerian forecourt system aimed at dispensing errors and cash leakage. PetroMunimji and SOFTGUN do meter-reading reconciliation, but their Nigerian reach is a vendor claim I did not confirm. An Odoo fuel-station module offers expiry alerts for legal documents and logs calibration litres. I did not check local renewal consultants (searched, none found).
result.duty: Fuel retail outlets must hold a valid NMDPRA operating licence, renewed through the ROMS portal (roms.nmdpra.gov.ng). A 2022 report says renewal needs an FIRS tax clearance certificate. Its validity period, fee and calendar were not found, so they are unverified. Separately, pumps need a Certificate of Verification from the Weights and Measures Department (Weights and Measures Act 2004). Stations without one, or with an expired one, have been sealed and prosecuted, but the validity period is not confirmed. NMDPRA's industry circular of about 22 Sep 2026 orders all outlets to calibrate and verify dispensers and totalisers immediately. It names no end date, and persistent or serious violations can lead to licence revocation. A N250,000 first-offence fine and 3-6 month revocation are reported only from an IPMAN Enugu communique, not NMDPRA's text. The circular names no record, log or certificate format.
result.market: NMDPRA had licensed 9,464 retail outlets as of 30 Apr 2024, per its Director-General as reported in the search results. In 2023 it estimated about 1,000 more unlicensed outlets. The 2025-2026 count was not found. IPMAN says its members run over 80-85% of filling stations, a self-reported share. Roughly 9,000-11,000 outlets carry the duty, most of them independents.
result.reason: The duties are real, but they are split across two agencies. NMDPRA's late-September 2026 circular orders outlets to calibrate and verify dispensers and totalisers, with licence revocation for serious breaches. It reads as a standing order, not a one-off. Pump verification certificates come from the Weights and Measures Department under the Weights and Measures Act 2004, and stations have been sealed for missing or expired ones. The operating licence is renewed on NMDPRA's own ROMS portal, which needs a tax clearance certificate. I found no product that tracks certificate and licence expiry for stations. The core work is physical recalibration and fixing tax papers, though, so software adds little. Fees and validity periods are not confirmed. Owners are reachable through IPMAN and PETROAN, but willingness to pay is doubtful.

result.duty: Lagos Health Sector Reform Law 2006: the HEFAMAA FAQ and portal say facility operators must register every year to operate. Registration covers hospitals, clinics, maternity centres, diagnostic centres and pharmacies, and the FAQ says it ends 31 Dec of each year. Failing to register brings a ₦100,000 fine when found, and the gazettengr report says 42 facilities were sealed in nine months. A first application needs a physical inspection, and renewal is done online. MLSCN Act 11 of 2003 requires lab registration and licensing, but the registrar calls ISO accreditation voluntary for now. I did not reach MLSCN's renewal fees or penalties. NHIA accreditation and re-accreditation (staff, equipment, infrastructure) is required to serve insurers. The Lagos insurance Executive Order of July 2024 has been enforced since Feb 2026, starting with state ministries and agencies. Uninsured residents are refused care at state-government facilities only.
result.market: About 4,127 private facilities in Lagos, out of roughly 5,000 recognised ones, per a HEFAMAA presentation from Nov 2023 (endmalaria.org). The NHIA network has more than 7,000 public and private facilities nationwide (PharmAccess 2024). Other states have similar agencies (Niger State: more than 1,000 facilities on its new portal).
result.reason: The duty is real. Every Lagos private health facility must register with HEFAMAA every year, with a ₦100,000 fine for not registering, and facilities keep being sealed. But the filing itself already runs through HEFAMAA's own free online portal. NHIA accreditation is also done online, using PharmAccess SafeCare tools. So software could only add a document vault, reminders and one tracker for all licences. I found no commercial tool doing that, only consultants. Two parts of the claim are overstated. MLSCN lab accreditation is voluntary for now, and the Ilera Eko rule refuses care only at state-government facilities, not private clinics. With about 4,100 facilities and a once-a-year task, pain and willingness to pay look modest. A done-for-you service fits better than SaaS.

Duty is real: CAC Form IT 4 for incorporated trustees, window 30 June to 31 December, with audited accounts. Fee reported at N5,000 plus N5,000 per year late, but that comes from a 2019 source. Non-filing blocks CAC post-incorporation services and can lead to strike-off. The CAC form cites s.848, but commentary cites other sections. No dedicated software was found in two searches; only the CAC portal, law-firm guides and accredited agents. I did not check market size (no register count) or enforcement against trustees. Score is low because the fees are small, congregations are unlikely to pay, audited accounts are the real cost, agents and lawyers already do the work, and filing is once a year.

Lagos State Safety Commission does enforce safety compliance certification. Leadership.ng reports 3,500+ construction sites certified, 641 hospitality audits, and sealing, stop-work and contravention notices for May 2025 to May 2026. But I found no official page on certificate cycle, fees, or statutory renewal frequency. The only fee data is the 2022 tech hub audit (N50k documentation plus N100k certification), which was suspended. I found no competing software, but the search was thin. The buyer set is mixed and the work is mostly physical (extinguishers, signage), so software only tracks documents. The market count is unclear and there is no clear recurring cycle. Weak, so low score.

The duty exists but is weak. The federal Co-operative Societies Act 1993 requires a member register and an annual audit by an auditor the society approves (s.36). It sets no fixed return deadline, since the Director sets returns under s.36(7). Fines are tiny (N1,000 or 6 months), and state laws were not checked. Competition exists, contradicting "none found": Clé Coop (First Registrars subsidiary, endorsed by Lagos State Ministry), the free Co-operative Apps, Wired-Banking software and KoopManager. Market: Lagos has over 10,000 registered societies but only about 2,000 are active (2019 BusinessDay). No national count was found. Many societies are informal, with low willingness to pay.

Duty is real: the Petroleum Industry Act 2021 s.199 requires an NMDPRA licence for retail outlets, and NMDPRA is sealing unlicensed LPG outlets (Akwa Ibom, Delta). The licence is a one-off or annual application filed on the NMDPRA portal (AGS/ELPS, LPG retailer Category D, Remita payment). That state portal already covers the core filing, and no commercial tracker was found. Market is roughly 2,000 registered versus 15,000 operating retailers (undated slide). Weaknesses: many operators are informal and unlicensed, willingness to pay is low, the reminder-only MVP is thin, and the idea overlaps the fuel-station candidate. I could not open the Guardian article (403), find the official checklist or fees, or see current penalties. Competitor search was shallow.

Duty is real: CAMA 2020 s.417 annual returns (companies within 42 days of AGM; business names by 30 June), and CAC's 15 Jul 2026 notice under s.692(3),(4) gives about 100,000 listed companies 90 days (about 13 Oct 2026, my own calculation) to file returns and PSC data. Search found only form templates (Paperform) and guides, with no bulk-filing tool. Market is large (about 3.1m registrations by 2019: 249k companies, 328k business names, 42k trustees). Weaknesses: the deadline is days away, so it is a one-off rush, and the list is mostly dormant firms unlikely to pay. The same 100,000 figure was announced in 2023. I did not check CAC portal agent access or fees. The letterhead rule (s.304(3)) is unchecked.

The duty is real. The PRA 2014 PCC is required of suppliers to federal bodies, and NSITF and ITF certificates are also required. But PenCom now runs a free online e-PCC portal (pcc.pencom.gov.ng, March 2026 guide). It issues the PCC at no cost, warns against third-party agents, and feeds daily PCC data to BPP. That kills the PCC part of a done-for-you service. NSITF is still manual: a request letter plus ECS forms, paid through Remita. No ITF portal was found. No dedicated tracker software surfaced, only consultants. The pain is episodic, since the three certificates are annual and only matter when bidding, and the buyers are small and price-sensitive. Market size was not reached, and I did not check whether non-government clients ask for the certificates. A thin reminder or checklist tool is possible, but willingness to pay looks low.

Duty is real. NTAA 2025 s.13 requires all taxable individuals, including the self-employed and informal earners, to file an annual return. LIRS set 31 March 2026, then extended it to 14 April. FCT-IRS extended to 30 April. Late filing is N100,000 for the first month and N50,000 for each later month under s.101, per press reports; I did not open the Act. No dedicated self-assessment app for sole proprietors turned up. The state portals (LIRS eTax, FCT) handle filing, and the market is mostly blogs and guides. Weaknesses: every state has its own portal and deadline (Edo files by emailed Form A), enforcement outside PAYE is weak, willingness to pay is low, and the next deadline is about March 2027. Cheap to distribute through accountants and bookkeepers. I did not find a register count of sole traders. I did not fetch the pages, so the "no app" finding rests on search snippets only.

The duty is real. The Nigerian Minerals and Mining Act 2007 has a chapter on possession and purchase of minerals, with sections on buying centres. Licences run through the Mining Cadastre Office's eMC+ portal, with fees paid via Remita. Titles are revoked for unpaid fees. I could not confirm a periodic returns or records duty for buyers, current renewal terms, or the current issuing ministry. No competing software was found, but eMC+ is the free state portal. The pool is tiny (about 91 gold licences, about 400 centres) and the state offtake channel (PAGMI to CBN) may sideline private buyers. The K15 rejection stands, so this is not a revive. Only 2 of 6 searches and no fetches were used.

The duty is real: annual Customs agent licence renewal, plus CRFFN practitioner licensing. The fee fight appears settled for now. A search summary says Customs kept the old fees in Feb 2026 (about N215,000, plus N15,000 per command) and shelved the N4m proposal. I did not open the pages, so this is unverified. I found no dedicated renewal software or state app, and no CRFFN app. The market is thousands of agents, but renewal happens once a year and is a simple form-and-fee task. Agents are fragmented, the pain is low, and ANLCA and CRFFN control the process. Willingness to pay is weak, and the digital route (B'Odogwu, National Single Window) may take over. B'Odogwu and market size were not checked.
